newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's 1996 wine harvest surpasses expectations.
newsitem.headline: France's 1996 wine harvest surpasses expectations.

text.p: France's 1996-vintage wines are turning out better than expected, rescued by two weeks of sunshine and cool breezes just before the start of the harvest, winemakers and other industry experts said on Sunday.
Some regions are still picking, but growers in most of the more prestigious areas are already predicting a fairly good to very good year.
The outlook is far better than a month ago, when growers in many regions were predicting a mediocre to average year at best due to heavy rains in late August.

The improved outlook should boost industry efforts to recover from international protests a year ago against Paris' nuclear testing programme, which dented French exports and tempted consumers to try wines from Australia and Chile.
The fear last month was that warm and wet weather would follow August's rains, encouraging rot which can drastically reduce yields as well as quality.
Instead, two weeks of cool and windy sunny weather set in over most of France.

Though there was sporadic rain during the harvest period, temperatures remained cool, staving off rot and resulting in some cases in wines with intense flavours and great ageing potential, growers and buyers agreed.
In particular, white Burgundies and Bordeaux reds -- some of France's most celebrated and costly wines -- could end up quite good this year, the experts said.

In Bordeaux, "I strongly believe that in 10 years, the 1996 vintage will be better than 1995," which was last year dubbed "the vintage of the century," said Jean-Christophe Esteve of the Caves Esteve in Paris.
"Many of the Burgundy whites will be extraordinary, with alcohol levels of 12 to 13 percent and relatively high acidity," Esteve told Reuters.

In Bordeaux's celebrated Medoc region, Jean-Guillaume Prats of Chateau Cos d'Estournel in Saint Estephe agreed. "This will be a very good year. The wines will be very classic, with extremely high levels of alcohol, acidity and tanin, which means wines with a great potential for ageing."
"The 1996s will start out more austere than the 1995s, but over the long term they could well prove greater," he said.
Consumers will have their first chance to test the new vintage after midnight on November 20 when this year's Beaujolais Nouveau is released in major world capitals.

In Beaujolais, "we are calling this the vintage rescued by a miracle," said Anne Mathon of the Beaujolais Wine Board. "At the start of September we had few expectations but the sunny weather turned things around."

In the southern Rhone valley, where the prized Chateauneuf du Pape and more common Cote du Rhone wines are made, 1996 quality "will be better than average" with average quantities, said Sylvie Reboul of the Cote du Rhone Winemakers Federation. "The growers are fairly satisfied," she said.

In the northern Rhone, home to the richly flavoured Hermitage and Cote Rotie wines, there will be great variation due to individual growers' timing, predicted winemaker Alain Graillot whose estate is near Tain-l'Hermitage.
"This will be a good year, not a great one," said Graillot. "Those who had the wisdom and the patience to wait before harvesting will be rewarded with wines of good acidity and good alcohol content."
